why: Qara Yusuf retook Tabriz and was independent of the Timurids from c.1408-1410; map wrongly shows Qara Qoyunlu under Timurid overlordship 1410-1430
Jahan Shah ruled as a Timurid vassal until Shah Rukh's death in 1447; map shows him independent in 1440
After 1447 Jahan Shah took Sultaniya, Qazvin, Rey and Hamadan; map keeps these Timurid until 1460/1470
Jahan Shah conquered Isfahan, Shiraz (Fars) and Yazd in the 1450s; map shows Timurids holding most of Iran (85-88%) in 1460-1470
Uzun Hasan destroyed the Qara Qoyunlu (1467-68) and defeated Timurid Abu Sa'id in 1469, taking western and central Iran; map shows Timurids still holding 88% of Iran in 1470

Treaty of Constantinople (1590) ceded Azerbaijan, Luristan, Kurdistan and Khuzestan but explicitly not Ardabil; Qazvin was the Safavid capital and Gilan was Safavid. Map gives all three to the Ottomans 1590-1600
Hotaki Afghans were expelled from Persia by Nader (Battle of Damghan, Sept/Oct 1729) and Tahmasp II restored; map still shows Hotaki holding 82% of Iran in 1730
Kabul was the Timurid appanage of Ulugh Beg Mirza II (1461-1502) until Babur took it in 1504; map labels it with the anachronistic modern province name 'Kapisa'

Afsharid authority in Afghanistan ended with Nader's death in 1747; Ahmad Shah Durrani held Kandahar and Kabul from 1747 and Herat from 1750. Map shows Afsharid Iran holding 77% of Afghanistan in 1750
Peshawar and the trans-Indus lands passed to Ahmad Shah Durrani after 1747; map shows Afsharid Iran in 1750
Lahore/Multan and Kashmir remained Mughal provinces until ceded to Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1752; map shows Afsharid Iran (Nader died 1747)
Punjab and Kashmir were Mughal until the 1752 cession to Durrani; Haryana was never Afsharid. Map shows Afsharid Iran in 1750
Ladakh was ruled by the Namgyal dynasty until the Dogra invasion of 1834; map flips it to Mughal (several decades), Afsharid Iran (1750), Durrani (1770) and Emirate of Afghanistan/Qing (1830)
Ladakh was conquered by the Dogras (1834-1842) and formed part of the Dogra state of Jammu and Kashmir from 1846; map shows stateless peoples (1850-60, 1880) and Qing (1870)
Ranjit Singh took Kashmir from the Durranis in 1819 and held it until 1846; map shows Emirate of Afghanistan in 1830
After 1765 the Sikh misls controlled the Punjab; map shows the Durrani Empire (1770) and the Mughal Empire (1780-90) there
Sikh misls held Lahore and central Punjab from 1765 until Ranjit Singh's takeover in 1799 (Multan stayed Durrani except 1772-80); map shows Durrani 1770 and Mughal Empire 1780-90
Durrani never held Haryana in 1770; the Delhi region remained under the Mughal court (later Maratha protection)
Sikh Empire held Lahore from 1799 and Multan from 1818 until British annexation in 1849; map shows Talpur (1820), Emirate of Afghanistan (1830) and Mughal remnants there
Peshawar was annexed by the Sikh Empire in 1834; map shows Durrani dynasty in 1840
British annexed the Punjab including Peshawar in 1849; map shows the Talpur dynasty of Sind in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in 1850
Peshawar region was British India 1849-1947; map shows the Talpur dynasty in parts of K.P. until 1880

Gilgit, Astore and Chilas were administered by Dogra Kashmir after the 1846 Treaty of Amritsar (Hunza and Nagar accepted Kashmiri suzerainty in the 1860s); map shows the Talpur dynasty of Sind here 1850-1880
These areas were British India (Gilgit Agency 1889, Kalat in subsidiary alliance 1876); map shows them under Afghanistan in 1890
Talpur Mirs ruled Sindh from 1783 until the British conquest of 1843; map shows Durrani Empire 1790-1810 and Sikh Empire in parts in 1840
Khanate of Kalat ruled most of Baluchistan (peak under Nasir Khan I 1749-94) until the 1876 Treaty of Kalat; map shows Afsharid Iran (1750), Talpur dynasty (1830) and British Empire (1850)
Goa remained Portuguese until India annexed it on 19 December 1961; map shows British India from 1890 and India from 1950

regions: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
why: Diu (1535) and Daman were Portuguese continuously until December 1961 (Dadra and Nagar Haveli 1783-1954); map flips the region to Gujarat (1550), Mughal (1580-1720), Maratha (1730-1810) and British (1820+)
Pondicherry, Karikal, Mahe and Yanam were French from 1816 until de facto transfer on 1 November 1954; map mislabels them 'French Indochina' (1860-80) and British India (1890-1950)
The Laccadive/Amindivi islands were under British India (Madras Presidency), never the Maldives; map shows them as Maldives from 1890
Lakshadweep joined India in 1947 and became a union territory in 1956; map shows it as part of the Maldives to 2025
These atolls were part of the Maldives sultanate, a British protected state 1887-1965; map shows them as 'no polity' from 1890 onward
Independent Maldives from 26 July 1965; map leaves these southern atolls as 'no polity' to 2025
Breakaway United Suvadive Republic in Addu, Huvadhu and Fuvahmulah 1959-1963 (apply after the protectorate row)
India has controlled the Siachen Glacier since Operation Meghdoot in April 1984; map shows Pakistan to 2025
No Sikkim state before Phuntsog Namgyal's consecration in 1642; map alternates a Gorkha Kingdom (1590, 1610, 1640) and Bhutan (1630) there
Sikkim was a British protectorate (Treaty of Tumlong 1861), not part of British India; map shows Tibet/Qing (1880) and British India (1890-1940)
Sikkim was an Indian protectorate from 1950 and merged into India only on 16 May 1975; map shows it as part of India from 1950

Bhutan was the Zhabdrung/Druk Desi dual-system state until Ugyen Wangchuck was elected monarch in December 1907; map uses the anachronistic 'Kingdom of Bhutan' from 1640 and puts Bhutan under the UK from 1890 (British control of foreign affairs began only with the 1910 Treaty of Punakha)
Wangchuck monarchy from 1907; British control of foreign relations only from the Treaty of Punakha (January 1910)
The Ahom kingdom was never part of the Toungoo empire; map gives Assam, Nagaland, Meghalaya and Arunachal to the First Toungoo Empire in 1570

After Itakhuli (1682) the Ahoms held the Brahmaputra valley up to the Manas until the Burmese invasions (1817) and British annexation (1826); map repeatedly gives Assam to Bhutan (1690, 1750, 1770, 1800-10) and the British (1770, 1810)

Manipur was an independent Meitei kingdom (zenith under Khagemba 1597-1652) until the Burmese invasions after 1751; map flips it to the 'First Toungoo Empire' (dynasty ended 1599) in 1610-20, 1640-60, 1690

The Naga hills were independent village polities until British consolidation from 1866 (HQ at Kohima 1878); map gives them to Toungoo (1570-1760), Konbaung (1770-80, 1810), Ahom (1820) and the British from 1830
The Lushai hills were ruled by Mizo chiefs until the British conquest of 1889-90; map gives them to Toungoo (1570-1760), Konbaung (1770) and the British from 1830

The tribal areas (Adi, Mishmi, Nyishi, etc.) were 'for all practical purposes independent' until the McMahon Line (1914); map assigns them to Toungoo, Bhutan, Konbaung, Qing (1800-80) and 'China' (1890-1910)

The Khasi/Jaintia hills were independent until the Anglo-Khasi War (1829-1833); map gives them to the Sur Empire, Toungoo, the Mughals (1590-1690), the Nawabs of Bengal (1750) and the British (1770-80, 1810)
Bengal broke away from the Sur Empire c.1553-55 (Muhammad Shahi dynasty) and was ruled by the Karrani dynasty 1564-1576 until the Mughal victory at Rajmahal; map keeps the Sur Empire to 1570
Independent Bengal sultanate (Muhammad Shahi then Karrani) 1553/55-1576; map shows Sur Empire 1560-1570
Karrani sultans held Bihar until the Mughal campaign of 1574 (ceded by Treaty of Katak); map shows Sur Empire 1560 and Mughal Empire 1570
Kotte (Prince Sapumal) conquered the Jaffna kingdom c.1450 and held it until 1467; map keeps Jaffna independent
Portuguese arrived 1505 seeking trade only; Kotte ruled the lowlands until its 1521 partition. Map shows Portuguese Ceylon/Portuguese Empire over most of the island from 1510
After the 1521 partition Kotte (Bhuvanekabahu VII) kept the western lowlands; no Portuguese territorial rule before 1597
Dharmapala's Kotte (Colombo and the Negombo-Galle coast) was a Portuguese client until his death in 1597, when direct Portuguese rule began
Sitawaka (1521-1594), based around Ratnapura/Ruwanwella, absorbed Raigama in 1538 and dominated the lowlands; absent from the map
Under Mayadunne and Rajasinha I Sitawaka held most of the island except Jaffna and the Portuguese coastal strip Negombo-Galle
Rajasinha I of Sitawaka conquered and held Kandy 1581/82-1591/92
Uva, Tamankaduwa, Vellassa/Batticaloa and Trincomalee were Kandyan, never Portuguese territory; map shows Portuguese Ceylon here from 1510

Uva, Tamankaduwa, Vellassa and Nuwarakalaviya were Kandyan provinces until the Kandyan Convention (1815); map gives them to Portuguese Ceylon, then Dutch Ceylon (1690-1790), then British Ceylon (1800-10)
East coast hinterland belonged to Kandy; Portuguese held only small forts here before the Dutch took Batticaloa (1638) and Trincomalee
Dutch captured Batticaloa (May 1638) and Trincomalee from the Portuguese; map keeps Portuguese Ceylon here to 1680
Sabaragamuwa and the Seven Korales were Kandyan provinces until 1815; map gives them to Portuguese, Dutch and British Ceylon
The Vanni chiefdoms (tributary to Jaffna) held the north-central dry zone; map shows Portuguese Ceylon here from 1510
Vanni chiefdoms remained autonomous through the Portuguese period; map shows Portuguese/Spanish rule from 1600
The Jaffna kingdom survived as a Portuguese client from 1591 until annexation in 1619; map shows Portuguese Ceylon from 1600
Portugal annexed Jaffna in 1619 and lost it in June 1658; map labels it 'Spanish Empire' (1620-30) and 'Portuguese India'
Jaffna and Mannar fell to the Dutch in 1658 and stayed Dutch until 1796; map shows Portuguese Ceylon in 1660
Direct Portuguese rule of the former Kotte lands from 1597; map labels this 'Spanish Empire' (1590-1630) — Portugal's colonies stayed Portuguese-administered under the Iberian Union
Portuguese direct rule of Colombo and the western lowlands 1597-1656
Galle was stormed by the Dutch on 13 March 1640 and the south coast remained Dutch until 1796; map shows Portuguese rule here until 1670
Colombo fell to the Dutch in 1656 and became their capital (1658); map shows Portuguese Ceylon in 1660
Ceylon was a separate Crown colony, never part of British India (Crown colony from 1802); map labels it 'British Raj' 1860-1880
One state (Dominion of Ceylon 1948-72) is split across two names ('Sri Lanka (Ceylon)' and 'Dominion of Ceylon') in 1950-1970
LTTE held the Vanni (Kilinochchi, Mullaitivu) as a de facto state for most of 1990-2009 (lost Kilinochchi Jan 2009, last territory 18 May 2009); map shows it only in 1990

Limbuwan (eastern Kirat hills) stayed independent until the Gorkha campaigns of 1772-1774; map gives it to the Sultanate of Bengal (1410-60, 1480, 1500-20), the Sur Empire (1540, 1560-70) and the Gorkha Kingdom from 1590
Makwanpur (Sen dynasty) held these hills until conquered by Prithvi Narayan Shah in 1762; map shows the Sur Empire (1540, 1560-70) and a Gorkha Kingdom from 1590
Kingdom of Parbat (founded 1436) was independent until the Nepalese invasion of 1786; map gives it to the Gorkha Kingdom from 1590
Sen kingdom of Palpa remained outside Nepal until Prithvi Pal Sen's death in 1806; map shows Delhi Sultanate (1510), Sur Empire (1540), Mughals (1560-70) and Gorkha from 1590

The Baise Rajya petty kingdoms (Salyan, Dang, Jajarkot, etc.) ruled the Bheri-Rapti hills until Gorkha annexation (Salyan and Dang 1786); map shows Jaunpur, Delhi, Sur, Mughal and a Gorkha Kingdom from 1590
Jumla, leading Baise state, was annexed by Gorkha in 1788-89; map gives it to the Gorkha Kingdom from 1590

Doti (Raika dynasty) ruled the far-west from the 13th century until its defeat by Gorkha in 1790 (Mughal action was only a raid); map shows Jaunpur, Delhi, Sur, Mughals and the Gorkha Kingdom from 1590
Abu'l-Khayr Khan (1428-1468) deposed the Sibir khan and ruled the steppe from Tyumen to the Syr Darya; map gives most of it to the Khanate of Sibir 1440-1480
Kesh/Karshi belonged to the Timurid kingdom of Samarkand until Shaybani's conquest (1500-01); the Kazakh Khanate never ruled it
Khatlon/Hisar was Timurid (Sultan Mahmud Mirza, Khusrau Shah) in 1480-1500; map shows the Kazakh Khanate

Muhammad Shaybani took Bukhara and Samarkand in 1500-01; map splits his state among 'Shaybanids', 'Shaybanid Khanate of Bukhara', 'Khanate of Bukhara' and still shows the Kazakh Khanate in Kashkadarya to 1510
Russia replaced khanal rule with okrug administration in the Middle (1822) and Junior (1824) jüz; map shows an independent Kazakh Khanate over 65% of Kazakhstan in 1830
Fergana valley remained the Khanate of Kokand (Russian vassal) until abolished in 1876; map shows Russian Empire from 1870
Bukhara became a semi-independent Russian vassal in 1868 and remained so until the revolution; map shows direct Russian rule 1870-1880 and 'Russia (Soviet Union)' as overlord from 1890
Eastern Bukhara (Khatlon) stayed under the Emir as a Russian protectorate; map shows direct Russian rule 1870-80
Chardzhou was a Bukharan bekdom; map gives it to Khiva (to 1870, 1890-1910) and direct Russian rule (1880)
Khiva became a Russian protectorate in 1873 and remained one until the revolution; map shows direct Russian rule in 1880
Dashoguz was Khivan territory under the 1873 protectorate; map shows direct Russian rule in 1880
Akhal Teke were independent until Skobelev took Geok Tepe (Dec 1880/Jan 1881) and Transcaspia was annexed in May 1881; map gives Ahal to Khiva 1830-70 and Russia in 1880
Merv was occupied by Russia only on 16 March 1884
Map labels Tsarist Central Asia 'Russia (Soviet Union)' from 1890; the USSR was founded only in 1922 and the Russian Empire ruled until 1917
